dashboard.description: The application plane: what HOPE itself is doing, as opposed to what the cluster underneath it is doing. Answers 'is the product working' — gateway throughput and latency, realtime transcription health, AI service behaviour, and background job outcomes. For node, storage, GPU and data-tier questions use the Infrastructure Overview, Node & System Activity, GPU and Data-tier Dependencies boards instead. Every connection/session number here is an application-level count; host socket counters live on the Node board and are not comparable.

panels.description: Scrape targets answering across the eight HOPE workloads (api-gateway, stt, stt-worker, text, guardrail, nlp, harness, tts). Anything below 8 is a service that is down or a scrape target whose address went stale — both read identically here, so check the Infrastructure Overview target table to tell them apart.
panels.title: HOPE services up

panels.description: HTTP requests per second served by the API gateway across all paths and methods. WebSocket frames are NOT counted here — realtime traffic is in the Realtime STT row.
panels.title: Gateway request rate

panels.description: Share of gateway responses that are 5xx. This is the gateway's own error budget: 4xx is excluded because a rejected request is usually the client's fault, and because the 404-over-403 tenancy posture makes 404 an expected, correct answer on cross-tenant reads.
panels.title: Gateway 5xx ratio

panels.description: 95th percentile end-to-end gateway request duration. Computed over the whole request population, so a slow admin export and a fast health probe share one number — use the per-path panel in the API Gateway row to attribute a rise.
panels.title: Gateway p95 latency

panels.description: Live client connections held by the API gateway process (`hope_api_active_connections_count`). This is the application's own count and is the number to quote when someone asks how many connections HOPE has. It is NOT `node_sockstat_sockets_used` on the Node & System board — that one counts every socket object on the whole k3s node, including UNIX-domain sockets belonging to kubelet and containerd, and idles near 940 with zero HOPE traffic.
panels.title: Open gateway connections

panels.description: Streaming transcription sessions currently held open by the STT service. A session survives a client reconnect (the gateway keeps it alive for a 15s grace window), so this counts consultations in progress, not sockets.
panels.title: Active STT sessions

panels.description: Gateway throughput split by HTTP status. Stacked, so the band height is total traffic and a widening red band is a regression. A steady 404 band is normal here: cross-tenant reads answer 404 by design rather than 403.
panels.title: Request rate by status

panels.description: p50 / p95 / p99 gateway request duration from the same histogram. A p99 that separates from p95 while p50 stays flat means a small population of slow requests — usually an unindexed query or a downstream AI call — not a general slowdown.
panels.title: Latency percentiles

panels.description: Top 10 routes by request rate. `path` is the Nest route template, not the resolved URL, so ids are already collapsed and this is safe to group by.
panels.title: Busiest paths

panels.description: Top 10 route+status pairs returning an error. Read alongside the status panel above: a 401 spike on an auth route is a client misconfiguration, the same spike on every route is an expired signing key.
panels.title: Failing paths (4xx / 5xx)

panels.description: Node.js event-loop delay percentiles for the gateway process. This is the honest saturation signal for a single-threaded runtime: CPU can read low while the loop is blocked. Sustained p99 above ~100ms means requests are queueing behind synchronous work.
panels.title: Event-loop lag

panels.description: V8 heap used against heap total, plus open file descriptors. A heap-used line that climbs monotonically across restarts is a leak; fds climbing with flat traffic means sockets or handles are not being released.
panels.title: Heap & file descriptors

panels.description: Error- and fatal-level log lines per service, from Loki (TASK-1180). The log-line contract reserves `error` for an operation that failed and may need someone to act, logged once, so a rising line here is a real failure, not chatter. The `ServiceLogErrorRateHigh` Loki rule tickets at more than 10 lines in 5 minutes for 10 minutes. Drill in: Explore on Loki with {service_name="<service>"} | detected_level="error", then follow hope_request_id or the TraceID link.
panels.title: Error log lines by service

panels.description: Concurrent streaming sessions, and new sessions per second. These are consultations, not sockets: one session survives many WebSocket reconnects.
panels.title: Sessions active & start rate

panels.description: Cumulative ASR processing seconds divided by audio seconds, per session, by engine. A live transcription system MUST sustain RTF below 1.0 — above it the engine is falling behind the microphone and latency grows without bound. The dashed line is 1.0.
panels.title: Real-time factor by engine

panels.description: Per-utterance ASR inference latency in streaming mode (p50/p95). Distinct from RTF: this is how long one utterance takes, RTF is whether the engine keeps up overall.
panels.title: Utterance inference latency

panels.description: Decoded audio seconds per session at teardown, by engine. Compare against wall-clock session duration: a large gap means sockets are being held open without audio flowing, which costs GPU residency and connection budget for nothing.
panels.title: Audio ingested per session

panels.description: Two independent quality faults. Dropped utterances: the per-session inference queue stayed full past the bounded enqueue wait, so an utterance is missing from the live transcript (the durable Redis audio path is unaffected). Script mismatch: a FINAL transcript came back in a script contradicting the session's pinned language — the engine returned confidently and the text published, so nothing else flags it.
panels.title: Transcript degradation

panels.description: Gateway WebSocket lifecycle from logs. `connected` is new sessions; `reconnected` is a client resuming an existing session inside the 15s grace window. Reconnects far exceeding connects means sockets are being dropped and redialled under a healthy-looking session count — on 2026-09-18 a fixed ~128s drop cadence produced 341 reconnects against 33 sessions.
panels.title: WebSocket session churn

panels.description: How streaming sessions terminate, parsed from the gateway finalize log. `session closed by client` is a clean shutdown. `grace window expired` means the client vanished and the 15s reaper collected it — a healthy client population should be mostly the former. Reads the top-level `reason` field from the structured JSON log line.
panels.title: Session end reason

panels.description: Gateway-side WebSocket faults: handshake rejections (bad ticket, unregistered origin, ownership mismatch), refused resumes, and egress-backpressure transcript drops. Any sustained non-zero value here is a client integration bug or an attack, not load. Scoped via the structured `context` field and the `detected_level` label.
panels.title: Session errors & rejections
Realtime STT — sessions, quality, socket churn

panels.description: LLM generations per minute by outcome. A `failed` band that tracks `completed` means the provider is rejecting or timing out a fixed share of calls — check provider health and the circuit breaker below before blaming the model.
panels.title: Text generation rate

panels.description: p50/p95 latency until the first token arrives. This is what a clinician actually perceives as responsiveness on a streaming summary — total generation time matters much less.
panels.title: Time to first token

panels.description: Generation speed in tokens per second (p50/p95) across providers. A drop with flat request volume usually means GPU contention on the in-cluster serving tier rather than a model change.
panels.title: Token throughput

panels.description: 1 = provider reachable, 0 = failing its health probe. Circuit-breaker state is 0 closed (traffic flowing), 1 half-open, 2 open (calls short-circuited). An open breaker means HOPE has stopped calling that provider entirely — requests fail fast rather than hanging.
panels.title: Provider health & circuit breakers

panels.description: Safety-engine verdicts per minute by decision. Guardrail owns policy and delegates inference to text and nlp, so a fall to zero here with healthy traffic elsewhere means screening is being skipped, not that content became safe.
panels.title: Guardrail decisions

panels.description: Queue depth and in-flight requests per admission gate, with p95 peer-call latency. Queue depth growing while in-flight is flat means the downstream peer (text or nlp) is the bottleneck.
panels.title: Guardrail saturation

panels.description: Per-batcher queue depth and p95 queue wait for the medical-NLP service. Wait time rising while depth stays low means batches are large but slow; both rising means the service is simply oversubscribed.
panels.title: NLP inference queue

panels.description: Generic FastAPI throughput for the services that expose no richer metrics of their own — harness and tts. This is deliberately thin: both are candidates for purpose-built metrics, and stt-worker exposes none at all beyond `up`.
panels.title: Python service request rate

panels.description: TASK-1181. Every note-writing generation that asked for English, by guard outcome, counted from the `text.output_language.guard` log line (exact, unlike the counter, whose first event per series is invisible to increase()). `clean`: no Malayalam. `repaired`: Malayalam found and the translate-only repair removed it. `unresolved`: the clinician got a note with Malayalam in it (repair failed or was rejected, or the note was streamed); this is what NoteLanguageUnresolved alerts on. `skipped`: guard disabled or a non-English target.
panels.title: Note language checks by outcome

panels.description: TASK-1181. Notes the guard found Malayalam in, per tenant id and agent: `repaired` were fixed before delivery, `unresolved` were delivered mixed. One agent that keeps appearing usually has a prompt that asks for Malayalam, so check the agent before the model. Tenant is read from the log line; it is deliberately not a metric label.

targets.expr: sum by (tenant_id, agent_slug, outcome) (count_over_time({service_name="hope-text", k8s_namespace_name=~".+"} |= "text.output_language.guard" | outcome=~"repaired|unresolved" [$__auto]))

panels.title: Mixed-language notes by tenant and agent

panels.description: TASK-1181. 95th percentile of Indic-script characters in a checked note BEFORE any repair, per model: how much Malayalam the model writes on its own. A rise here with flat `unresolved` means the repair is absorbing a model or prompt regression; a rise in both means it no longer can. 0 is the target.
panels.title: Malayalam characters per note before repair (p95)

panels.description: BullMQ jobs currently being processed, per queue. A queue pinned at its concurrency limit with a growing wait time below is a backlog forming.
panels.title: Jobs in flight by queue

panels.description: Completed vs failed jobs per minute by queue. Failures here are silent to the user who triggered them — a DNA report or webhook that never arrives produces no HTTP error.
panels.title: Job outcome rate

panels.description: Failures grouped by exception class. `ServiceUnavailableException` points at a downstream AI service; a Prisma validation error points at schema or seed drift in the database, not at load.
panels.title: Job errors by type

panels.description: p50/p95 time a job spends waiting before a worker picks it up. Rising wait with flat failure rate means not enough worker capacity; both rising means workers are crash-looping.
panels.title: Job queue wait
